result:
Morning always feels like a decision. The first light slips through the blinds in thin, polite stripes, as if it’s asking permission to enter. I lie still and listen to the house settle—the soft click of pipes, the distant hum of a neighbor’s refrigerator—until the day becomes real enough to touch.

I think about how we spend so much time waiting for the future, even though the future is made of moments that arrive without ceremony. A bus sighs at the curb. Someone laughs too loudly in a hallway. A stranger drops a coin and bends to retrieve it with the care of a person handling something fragile. Nothing dramatic happens, and yet the world keeps offering small proofs that it is alive.

Outside, the street is damp from an earlier rain. The pavement looks like dark glass, reflecting storefront signs that are too bright for the hour. I watch a leaf drift along the gutter, caught and released by the current, as if the wind is practicing a slow form of patience.

Eventually I get up. I make coffee that tastes slightly different each morning, never quite the same twice, even when I use the exact same grounds. I tell myself this is practice: learning to meet what comes without demanding it be familiar.

By the time the kettle clicks off, I’m ready to move through the day. Not because everything is solved, but because the next thing—whatever it is—has already started waiting for me.
